Introducing AMD Helion, Agentic AI Compute at Rack Scale :: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD)
Press Release
Introducing AMD Helion, Agentic AI Compute at Rack Scale
October 12, 2026 9:00 am EDT
Download as PDF
News Highlights:
AMD Helion lets customers tailor CPU core density, performance and power to agentic workloads, with CPU-only configurations for hyperscale deployments and integrated CPU/GPU configurations for enterprises.
AMD Helion combines open hardware and software with an integrated token router that directs agents’ model calls across frontier and open-source models.
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Oct.  12, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) --
AMD
(NASDAQ: AMD) today introduced the AMD Helion agentic AI rack, an open blueprint for agentic AI infrastructure based on an Open Compute Project spec-design and powered by AMD compute.
Building on the open-platform approach of the AMD Helios™ rackscale solution, AMD Helion is designed to provide partners and customers with the flexibility they need for agentic AI infrastructure. With AMD Helion, customers can match CPU performance, core density and power with GPU acceleration for the work their AI agents perform.
“Agentic AI is not a single workload. It spans personal agents, enterprise applications, code execution and complex workflows, each with different compute requirements,” said Dan McNamara, senior vice president and general manager, Compute and Enterprise AI, AMD. “To do that takes optimized compute and infrastructure that can adapt to different workloads. With AMD Helion, we are bringing AMD EPYC™ performance, open software and flexible rack designs together so our partners can build systems around customer needs and make efficient use of available power.”
AMD Helion’s OCP spec-based rack blueprint supports open software and can come in flexible configurations, including liquid- and air-cooled versions, allowing customers to create virtually any configuration needed for their needs. Some examples of this include:
A CPU-only rack powered by 6th Gen AMD EPYC™ processors that can support up to 32,768 CPU cores. This rack is designed for hyperscale customers, providing dedicated capacity for agent execution and connections to separate model inference infrastructure.
An all-in-one rack that combines AMD EPYC CPU nodes, AMD Instinct™ MI350P GPU nodes and general-purpose compute on one platform. This rack is designed to provide partners and customers an all-in-one concept for enterprise agentic AI.
AMD Helion enables customers to deploy agentic AI in the IT infrastructure they already have, turning existing investments into a foundation for new AI capabilities. Partners can tailor CPU and GPU configurations to customer workloads, matching agent execution, model inference and supporting compute to each deployment’s performance, power and cost requirements.
AMD plans to contribute the AMD Helion specification to OCP, making it available to the community for further development and adoption. AMD Helion agentic rack configurations are currently under development with ecosystem partners and are planned to be available in November 2026.
Ecosystem Support
AMD is helping shape the next phase of AI infrastructure through open, flexible platforms, a broad portfolio of workload-optimized compute and collaboration across the ecosystem. AMD Helion brings that approach to agentic AI, helping partners match software and compute to the work agents perform and giving customers flexibility to scale as their requirements evolve.
“Agentic AI is changing what customers need from their infrastructure. It's not just about compute performance, but how the entire system is connected, managed and secured. Architectures like AMD Helion, combined with Cisco's full-stack infrastructure capabilities, can give customers greater flexibility to deploy, operate and scale agentic workloads into their environments as their needs evolve.” -
Jeremy Foster, Senior Vice President and General Manager, Cisco Compute
“Dell PowerRack gives customers choice without compromise, and our support for AMD Helion Agentic Rack Reference Design extends that promise to the next generation of agentic AI. By combining AMD's rack-scale architecture with Dell's proven engineering expertise, along with the flexibility to extend deployments with Dell PowerRack for Networking and Storage, we're giving customers a complete, validated path to deploy agentic compute at scale with the manageability and reliability they expect from Dell.” -
Arun Narayanan, Senior Vice President, Compute and Networking, Dell Technologies
“Hon Hai Technology Group continues to deepen its collaboration with AMD on AI infrastructure, supporting the new AMD Helion Agentic AI Rack reference design. Built on an open architecture, the platform combines 6th Gen AMD EPYC processors with flexible CPU and GPU configurations to address hyperscale data center and enterprise Agentic AI workloads. The Group will continue to leverage its strengths in rack-level system integration and global manufacturing, working with ecosystem partners to advance rack-scale Agentic AI solutions and accelerate next-generation AI infrastructure deployment.” –
Hon Hai Technology Group
“Next-generation AI workloads require scale, efficiency, and flexibility that open, rack-scale architectures deliver, as demonstrated by our recent customer agreement to deploy AMD Helios. For decades, HPE and AMD have jointly championed open standards, and we are continuing to advance those efforts with AMD Helion. Together, we are ushering in the next era of AI with open large-scale systems, enhanced with air-cooled and direct liquid-cooled networking, supported by decades of HPE expertise and innovation.” –
Trish Damkroger, Senior Vice President and General Manager, HPC & AI Infrastructure Solutions, HPE
“As agentic AI moves into production, customers need flexibility in how and where they deploy it. That’s at the core of the Lenovo Hybrid AI Advantage, and AMD Helion will give added versatility to meet customers where they are and support the workloads they want to run.” -
Scott Patti, VP, Infrastructure Solutions Group, Lenovo
“Agentic AI will require a range of system designs to serve different customer needs. AMD Helion provides an open blueprint that gives QCT the flexibility to tailor compute configurations and bring system design and customization expertise to those requirements.” - Mike Yang, President of QCT
“Supermicro is accelerating the deployment of next-generation agentic AI infrastructure by bringing AMD’s Helion - the open, ORv3 compliant rack-scale architecture to market through our Data Center Building Block Solutions® (DCBBS). With our proven expertise in OCP accepted™ rack-scale design, integration, liquid cooling, software, and deployment services, we transform advanced Agentic AI architectures into production-ready solutions. Together with AMD, we enable customers to deploy faster, scale efficiently, and accelerate time to online for agentic AI.” -
Vik Malyala, Chief Business Officer, Supermicro
“AMD Helion provides an open, flexible foundation for agentic AI infrastructure. Wiwynn is excited to collaborate with AMD, bringing our expertise in rack-level integration and advanced cooling to help hyperscaler customers tailor systems that meet the demanding workloads, power requirements, and data center environments of the agentic AI era.” -
William Lin, President and CEO, Wiwynn

items.title: Preparing for the 2026 US midterms
items.content:
Preparing for the 2026 US midterms \ Anthropic
Skip to main content
Skip to footer
Try Claude
Policy
Preparing for the 2026 US midterms
Oct 14, 2026
Earlier this year, we shared an
update on our election safeguards
, which described how we measure and prevent political bias, detect misuse, and direct people to accurate voting information.
Below, we outline how we've built on that work and continued to strengthen our election safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms.
How people use Claude for elections and politics
Our goal is for Claude to be a useful tool for political conversations, while preventing election-related abuse. That starts with understanding how people actually use Claude in these contexts. To do this, we used Anthropic Insights to develop a new analysis of 250,000 conversations over the course of a recent one-week period.
1
Today, conversations that touch broadly on politics, public policy, or social issues account for about 5.75% of all conversations in the United States on Claude.ai, our consumer app. This includes people turning to Claude to follow the news, conduct academic or professional research on public policy, learn about candidates, and navigate government services. About 0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting. As we get closer to Election Day, we expect the share of political and election-related queries to
increase
.
This sample suggests people rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for. These kinds of requests showed up in about 0.01% of US Claude conversations. More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our
election integrity policies
were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations.
2
How many US Claude.ai conversations touch on politics, are about elections, or ask Claude whom or what to vote for.
Each dot represents 1 in every 10,000 conversations in a random sample of about 250,000 US Claude.ai consumer conversations from September 21 to 27, 2026, which Claude classified using
a privacy-preserving method
. Because requests for a recommendation on whom or what to vote for are so rare, we show the upper end of a 95% confidence interval for that group. Examples are illustrative only. Most of the requests we see are informational in nature. People turn to Claude to make sense of geopolitical events, research candidates, draft documents, assist with coursework, and weigh arguments for and against policies.
What people ask Claude for in political conversations.
Conversations were clustered in a privacy-preserving, bottom-up manner through
Anthropic Insights
.
Connecting people to trusted sources
Ahead of Election Day, we've added two ways for people to get reliable information directly in their conversations with Claude. As we shared in April, when people ask Claude.ai about voter registration, polling places, or election dates, we’ll continue to display a banner linking to TurboVote, a nonpartisan resource from
Democracy Works
.
Later this month, Claude will start drawing official voting information from Democracy Works into its responses on Claude.ai for users in the US. Someone asking where to vote or what ID to bring to their polling place will now get an answer specific to their state, without leaving the conversation. These responses draw on publicly available information that Democracy Works collects from state and local election sources.
Official voting information presented by Democracy Works.
Additionally, Claude will begin showing up-to-date results on election night and in the days that follow, so that when people ask for current vote counts or election results, they'll be shown the latest official numbers directly in their conversation.
Measuring and preventing political bias
When people ask Claude about politics, they should get accurate and evenhanded answers that don't favor any particular political viewpoint. That’s why we test our models extensively for political bias before every model launch. Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 are our most evenhanded to date, scoring 99% on our
political evenhandedness evaluation
.
Our latest models also engage more readily with political discussions and decline fewer requests, so people can get the information they came for. We're continuing to refine these evaluations, and also looking beyond them for new ways to pressure-test how our models handle political topics.
As part of that effort, we asked three independent groups to review how Claude handles free expression, each from a different angle with different methodologies.
The Future of Free Speech
, an independent think tank at Vanderbilt University, tested Claude on hundreds of requests on contentious topics, and the
Foundation for American Innovation
compared how Claude responded to matched prompts from the left and right, ranging from mainstream policy debates to more extreme scenarios. On both of these evaluations, most of the responses were rated as strong, engaging substantively with requests. The
Collective Intelligence Project
surveyed more than 2,000 people in the US, UK, and India in developing an evaluation. Through a three-stage process, participants proposed principles for handling sensitive topics, ranging from health to politics, identified topics to test, and helped develop criteria for judging model responses. CIP synthesized this input and tested for agreement across demographic and cultural groups to establish shared principles.
These evaluations also identified areas where Claude still falls short. The Future of Free Speech and the Collective Intelligence Project both found that Claude rarely refused requests, but sometimes added unsolicited caveats and counterarguments, such as inserting an opposing view into an advocacy email. And the Foundation for American Innovation found that Claude Sonnet 4.5 didn’t always hedge evenly, and was more likely to soften arguments for right-leaning positions.
We're addressing this in a few ways. We've improved how Claude responds to direct yes-or-no questions and requests for shorter answers, where we found its answers could be less balanced. We're also using these findings to improve when and how Claude adds caveats or counterarguments, so it treats requests from across the political spectrum more consistently. And we're continuing to improve how we test for uneven hedging, building on existing evaluations that use matched prompts from the left and right. More broadly, we're working to expand our political bias evaluations to better reflect real conversations and to cover candidates and voting questions as well as policy issues.
How we define misuse
Our
Usage Policy
prohibits using Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections, from spreading false information about candidates or how to vote, to impersonating election officials or trying to suppress turnout. Each year, we update the policy to reflect our models’ evolving capabilities and feedback from our customers. This year’s update, which we
announced
last week, clarifies what our election rules cover and what they don't, and adds new examples to help people understand where the lines fall.
We know many political campaigns use Claude for legitimate, everyday tasks, so we recently
published a guide
to help them understand where these policies apply. It covers the many ways campaigns can put Claude to work, such as drafting press statements and fundraising emails, prepping for debates, analyzing turnout data, and building voter outreach materials. It also spells out what’s prohibited, such as using Claude to create fake social media profiles that pose as real people, mass-producing comments to inflate a campaign’s engagement, or writing content for news sites and pages that falsely claim to be independent.
Testing and strengthening our defenses
We deploy automated classifiers that are trained to detect election-related abuse. To see how these safeguards hold up in practice, we partnered with the
Institute for Strategic Dialogue
(ISD) and the
McCain Institute
, both independent research organizations, to pressure-test our protections in the US, Israel, and Brazil. Analysts tested whether Claude would assist with deceptive campaigning, misinformation, and other forms of election abuse. They began with direct requests, then broke full campaigns into smaller tasks that could look harmless on their own, such as audience research, building news sites, drafting content, and planning its distribution. They found that Claude reliably refused a single harmful request, but could miss a malicious campaign when it was spread across many individual requests that looked harmless on their own.
Building on these findings and our own, we've added new classifiers to better identify novel and multi-step misuse, including attempts to build fake social media accounts and news sites aimed at political discussions, or to run financially motivated election schemes. We also enhanced our ability to detect election-related misuse by foreign state actors, and strengthened our cyber protections for election infrastructure and campaigns. Finally, we built targeted safeguards for localized risks identified in the US, Israel, and Brazil, which all have major national elections this year.
Our threat intelligence and enforcement teams review flagged activity and take action when they confirm a violation, including banning accounts. We also routinely share
examples
of unintended model actions or behavior we've observed during our evaluations and internal use of Claude.
What we've found
Our recent
threat intelligence report
reflects a broader shift in election-related abuse trends. Political, state-aligned, and commercial actors are now incorporating AI into nearly every aspect of their influence operations, from planning and content creation to building platforms used to disseminate a message. Because we see these early stages of an operation happening on Claude, we often have a chance to stop these efforts before they ever reach the public.
Our teams have continued to investigate and prevent coordinated abuse around elections, including the US midterms. In one case, foreign-based operators of a fake news site used Claude to produce US midterm coverage favoring Russian, Iranian, and North Korean narratives. We've also observed threat actors seeking to exploit the election for financial gain, using Claude to produce fabricated news and other content designed to attract American audiences and generate advertising revenue. We banned the accounts involved in these cases and improved our ability to detect this type of abuse.
Looking ahead
More people are turning to Claude for information about this year’s elections than ever before. We have a responsibility to make sure the answers they get are accurate and balanced, and that Claude isn’t used to undermine the democratic process. We’ll continue to invest in making Claude more evenhanded, preventing and addressing misuse, and being transparent in our actions. This work will be critical in the upcoming US midterms and extends to elections around the world as well. In the coming months, we also hope to share a more comprehensive look at how people used Claude throughout the election cycle, with the goal of strengthening our election-related evaluations and safeguards.
Footnotes
We took a random sample of 250,000 US Claude.ai consumer conversations from September 21 to 27, 2026 and analyzed them in a privacy-preserving way.
This figure was generated from a separate analysis of 250,000 Claude.ai conversations, which were reviewed against our election integrity policy.

items.content:
Singapore office and government MOU | Anthropic \ Anthropic
Skip to main content
Skip to footer
Try Claude
Announcements
Anthropic opens Singapore office and signs MOU with the Government of Singapore
Oct 14, 2026
Today, we are expanding our Asia-Pacific operations by opening a new office in Singapore—our fifth in the region—and signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Singapore Ministry of Digital Development and Information. Singapore is one of our most active markets anywhere in the world, and Claude is already powering Singaporean business and government services used by millions of people every day, like GovTech Singapore, Grab, and DBS. Our growing local team will ensure these organizations and many more stay on the frontier with safe, capable AI.
“We’re committed to Singapore for the long term,” said Dale Finlay, General Manager of ASEAN at Anthropic. “Our customers here hold AI to an extremely high standard, especially when it comes to reliability and security. Having a team on the ground means we can get even closer to the organizations putting Claude to work on their hardest problems.”
Supporting responsible AI in Singapore
Kai Fong Chng, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann signed the MOU on the sidelines of Singapore International Cyber Week. Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo and Michael Sellitto, Anthropic Head of APAC Policy, witnessed the signing. It sets out areas of cooperation in AI safety, security, and model evaluation; research on AI adoption and its impact; and responsible adoption across the public and private sectors.
“Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Mann. “We founded Anthropic on the belief that capability and safety have to go hand in hand. With this MOU, we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world.”
“Singapore’s approach to AI has always been to enable innovation while keeping pace with its evolving risks. Trust is critical for businesses, workers, and the public to use AI with confidence,” said Chng. “This partnership with Anthropic reflects the Government’s commitment to scaling up the responsible adoption of AI, deepening capabilities in our companies and government agencies, and delivering impact for Singapore.”
Our work with Singapore goes back to 2023, when we joined the
Generative AI Evaluation Sandbox
run by the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the AI Verify Foundation. We later partnered with them on a
red-teaming project
in English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil.
Under the MOU, we plan to hold technical exchanges with Singapore’s AI safety, security, and assurance institutions on model evaluation, testing standards, and incident response. We do similar work with safety institutes around the world, where sharing technical information provides governments with a clearer view of frontier AI capabilities and risks, while helping developers build safer models.
We’ll also look for ways to strengthen AI skills in Singapore, help small and medium-sized businesses adopt AI responsibly, and support the government’s goal of building AI capability among public officers. We plan to share research and data with the government, including from the
Anthropic Economic Index
, and to offer technical and policy expertise as Singapore develops its rules for AI.
How Singapore is working with Claude
In our latest
Economic Index
, Singapore ranks second of 121 countries in Claude.ai usage relative to its population, at nearly six times what its size alone would predict.
In the public sector, more than 1,500 engineers and technical staff at the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) have adopted Claude Code to modernize government systems and speed up software delivery. This has helped GovTech Singapore teams build, maintain, and enhance digital services more efficiently at national scale. The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore is exploring how Claude could help strengthen the country’s cyber defense.
In financial services, DBS, Southeast Asia’s largest bank, works with Claude across a range of use cases in its Singapore operations—including software development and day-to-day productivity—as part of its broader AI innovation efforts. These applications operate within the bank’s strict security and governance framework. GIC, Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, is rolling out Claude across its investment and corporate services teams. Organizations in regulated sectors like financial services can now run Claude with
in-region inference
on Amazon Bedrock, helping them meet strict data processing requirements.
Singapore’s largest technology companies and startups are building with Claude too. Grab powers BriX, its sales assistant, with Claude. The assistant saves Grab’s sales teams approximately 40,000 hours every quarter and surfaces new sales opportunities. Sea—the business behind Shopee, Garena, and Monee—works with Claude to help Shopee’s customer service chatbot respond faster and more accurately, and thousands of its employees write and debug code with Claude. And Supabase—the developer platform with strong roots in Singapore—is building with Claude Code.
Building with the developer community
This week, senior leaders from Anthropic are in Singapore to open the office and meet with customers, developers, and policymakers.
Today, we hosted Builder Summit Singapore, bringing more than 300 developers together with engineering and product leaders from Anthropic. Earlier in the week, Singapore’s Claude community ambassadors held a meetup for more than 700 local builders.
Our Singapore office is now open and hiring. To learn more about joining the team, visit our
careers page
.

AI-Generated Summary
NVIDIA NeMo Gym
provides an open evaluation environment that diagnoses failure modes and tracks error propagation across multistage chip design workflows.
The Siemens Fuse EDA AI Agent used NeMo Gym to evaluate and improve Liberty file generation for standard-cell characterization, increasing the composite verification score from approximately 55% to ~95% across a representative benchmark.
Agent turns decreased from 155 to 53 and output tokens fell from approximately 81K to 29K after refining skills and Model Context Protocol tool descriptions based on verifier diagnostics.
A domain-specific verifier checks coverage, validity, relative validation, accuracy, and integrity of final Liberty artifacts, assigning zero reward if any gate fails.
The same evaluation method applies to engineering agents in EDA, CAE, and other domains by grading final artifacts and optimizing skills through repeated rollouts.
Next Steps
Run the
NeMo Gym Quickstart
to begin evaluating agents on a representative task.
Watch the
Self-Verifying, Long-Running Agentic Characterization Workflow Demo
for a detailed walkthrough of the Solido Fuse approach.
Learn more about the
collaboration between NVIDIA and Siemens
on industrial AI for chip design.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
AI agents
offer remarkable productivity gains in complex chip design workflows, but their tendency to generate plausible yet incorrect artifacts makes reliability a major barrier to production adoption. In multistage engineering workflows, an undetected error early in setup can silently propagate through downstream stages and final artifact generation. Evaluating and refining these agents against verified final outputs, rather than isolated intermediate steps, is essential for building trustworthy automation.
NVIDIA NeMo Gym
, an open library for evaluating and improving models and agents using environments, addresses this challenge. The NeMo Gym agentic evaluation environment is designed to diagnose failure modes and track error propagation across complex, multistage workflows. By establishing a domain-specific verifier to inspect final outputs against verified reference artifacts, NeMo Gym enables engineers to trace complete rollout trajectories and identify root causes behind subtle errors.
This post walks through how NeMo Gym was used to evaluate and improve the reliability of the
Siemens Fuse EDA AI Agent
when calling characterization tools. The Siemens Fuse team used NeMo Gym to scale up evaluations and verify the resulting Liberty (.lib) files against known references and tracing—both common and rare failures through each rollout. Those findings guided changes to the agent’s skill and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool descriptions, increasing the measured benchmark composite score from approximately 55% to ~95% across a benchmark of representative standard-cell characterization tasks, while reducing turns and output tokens.
Siemens’ work provides a practical example for chip design teams and EDA developers on how to leverage the NVIDIA AI software stack and open libraries to improve agent reliability and chip design workflows.
Automating standard-cell characterization
Standard-cell characterization is the process of generating accurate timing, power, and noise models for logic cells across operating conditions. It is foundational to chip design and required whenever a semiconductor foundry issues a new process design kit (PDK). Each new PDK carries SPICE transistor models; design rules; and process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) definitions that connect the manufacturing process to design tools. When a foundry updates a PDK, existing characterization datasets may no longer accurately describe the updated devices. Timing and power models must then be regenerated and validated for every affected cell across combinations of input slew, output load, and PVT conditions.
The Solido Characterization Suite agent automates this process. The agent orchestrates tools from the broader
Solido Characterization Suite
through Siemens Fuse EDA AI Agent, which exposes MCP servers and skills to common coding harnesses including Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.
MCP interfaces make these accelerated tools accessible to engineering agents, while skills guide their use in characterization workflows. Faster simulation helps agents complete engineering iterations sooner, while NVIDIA NeMo Gym helps developers measure and improve how reliably and efficiently agents orchestrate those tools.
The Solido Characterization Suite agent must perform tool setup, large-scale SPICE simulation, distributed compute, Liberty file generation, debugging, and final validation (Figure 1). Errors often produce plausible outputs instead of clean failures, leaving incorrect thresholds, missing corners, or incomplete cells hidden. Because these stages depended on one another, an early setup error could propagate into every step that followed. Defining a rigorous evaluation protocol was a key step in preparing the Solido Characterization Suite agent for production workflows.
Figure 1. Agentic characterization workflow from SPICE inputs through pilot validation, scale-out, Liberty generation, and waveform comparison. Early setup errors propagate to the final library
Measuring and improving agent reliability with NeMo Gym
Part of the
NVIDIA NeMo
collection of open libraries for agent specialization and optimization, NeMo Gym integrates with the standard-cell characterization flow inside a controlled evaluation loop (Figure 2). It defines the task, tools, state, and verifier for each rollout so that attempts started from a clean state and produced comparable results. It also records thinking traces, input and output messages, and tool actions.
This enabled engineers to run the following optimization loop:
Run baseline rollouts with a versioned task and verifier in a custom NeMo Gym environment
Inspect trajectories, failed tool calls, and verifier diagnostics
Identify ambiguous instructions, unproductive actions, and incorrect tool selection
Refine the agent’s skills and MCP tool descriptions
Repeat the same tasks under the same evaluation conditions
Compare verified outcomes and efficiency per successful result
Figure 2. NeMo Gym checks the Liberty files produced by the Solido Characterization Suite agent and Solido tools, then feeds failure analysis into the next skill and tool-description revision. The entire process is driven by a coding agent with a human in the loop
Reward design and artifact verification
As the team analyzed agent trajectories, end-to-end evaluation uncovered failures that intermediate checks missed. For example, final Liberty verification exposed missing cells and operating conditions, incorrect slew thresholds, and timing or power values outside tolerance. These findings show why engineering agents must be evaluated against final artifacts rather than individual tool calls.
To make the work repeatable, the team implemented verifiers that provide a final composite reward score based on the following metrics:
Coverage
: Whether the agent produced every expected cell and PVT corner.
Validity
: Whether the delivered Liberty files are well-formed and usable by the validation tools.
Relative validation:
Whether the output introduced failures beyond those already present in the reference.
Accuracy
: The fraction of expected timing and power values that falls within the defined tolerance.
Integrity
: Whether the characterization workflow produced the complete result rather than reusing, truncating, or reformatting existing values.
The reward score is defined as:
\(R=\mathbf{1}\left[\text{Coverage}\right]\times\mathbf{1}\left[\text{Validity}\right]\times\mathbf{1}\left[\text{Relative Validation}\right]\times\mathbf{1}\left[\text{Integrity}\right]\times\frac{X_{\text{tol}}}{X_{\text{total}}}\)
Here, \(X_{\mathrm{tol}}\) is the number of values in the output that are within tolerance, and \(X_{\mathrm{total}}\) is the total number of output values. Their ratio represents the fraction of output values within tolerance.
Each indicator \(\mathbf{1}[\cdot]\) equals \(1\) when its corresponding gate passes and \(0\) when it fails. The reward is zero if any gate fails.
Using this verifier, the team systematically evaluated and tuned the agent’s performance across multiple iterations.
Optimizing the agent
The team used the
open source GF180MCU PDK
to benchmark the Solido Characterization Suite agent on Liberty-file generation. The dataset includes 229 standard cells across 36 PVT corners, using Solido AFS for SPICE simulation.
A custom agentic environment was built using NeMo Gym. For each run, the characterization flow was restricted to two cells across 36 PVT corners, as this smaller subset was sufficient for tuning the agentic workflow. Each run took approximately 1.5 to 2 hours, and the team conducted approximately 25 rollouts using Claude Opus 4.8 running in Claude Code as the fixed model and agent harness.
Across successive evaluation rounds, the team refined the agent’s characterization skills and MCP tool descriptions. To improve tool selection, they simplified overlapping file and shell interfaces and defined tool inputs with explicit JSON schemas, making characterization tools easier for the agent to call.
Following these refinements, the mean composite verification score across evaluated rollouts increased from approximately 55% to 95%. The improved workflow also required fewer agent turns and output tokens. Agent turns fell from 155 to 53, a reduction of approximately 66%, while output tokens fell from approximately 81K to 29K, a reduction of approximately 64%.

Developing reliable agents in other domains using the same method
The same evaluation method applies to engineering agents in EDA, CAE, and other engineering domains:
Evaluate the final engineering artifacts and not just whether individual tool calls succeeded.

How to Rewrite Apache Spark UDFs for GPU Acceleration with AI Agents
Oct 13, 2026
By
Rishi Chandra
and
Erik Ordentlich
Like
Discuss (0)

T
F
R
E
AI-Generated Summary
NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark
leverages GPU parallelism to accelerate data analytics workloads and improve total cost of ownership.
User-defined functions in Spark break the declarative abstraction, forcing GPU-accelerated pipelines to fall back to CPU execution and incur data transfer overhead.
UDFs can be rewritten using Spark SQL expressions, the RapidsUDF interface with the
Java API for cuDF
, or custom CUDA kernels via JNI to eliminate fallback and achieve over 20x speedups.
The
cuDF skills for Apache Spark
provide agent-driven workflows that guide testing, conversion, benchmarking, and optimization with verification-driven feedback loops.
A major consumer technology company converted more than 30 production UDFs using this workflow, with one rewrite reducing operator time from 274.55 to 12.78 hours across a 600-billion-row workload.
Next Steps
Install the
cuDF skills for Apache Spark
to begin rewriting UDFs with agent assistance.
Watch the
Data + AI Summit session on coding AI agents for Spark UDF GPU acceleration
for a deeper walkthrough.
Follow the
cuDF plugin for Apache Spark getting-started guide
to enable GPU acceleration in Spark pipelines.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
Enterprise applications have become increasingly demanding. Agentic AI has compounded the need for vast amounts of enterprise data with frequent, complex queries across increasingly large datasets.
Meeting that demand requires greater data throughput without a proportional increase in cost.
NVIDIA cuDF
addresses this challenge by leveraging the massive parallelism and high-bandwidth memory of GPUs for data analytics. Particularly, the
NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark
brings this acceleration to
Apache Spark
, the industry-leading platform for big data processing and analytics, to achieve
better TCO performance
in major workloads.
User-defined functions (UDFs)
have long been problematic for accelerated query engines,
introducing runtime overheads due to their opaque nature. While UDFs can often be replaced with more performant code, rewriting UDFs has long been a laborious process requiring careful validation.
This post describes how to use agents to rewrite UDFs into GPU-accelerated equivalents within minutes, achieving 22x+ speedups in Apache Spark jobs
. We’ll introduce the
cuDF skills for Apache Spark
, a set of skills to quickly break through the UDF bottleneck for end-to-end development, from testing, to benchmarking, through integration.
The UDF challenge
cuDF achieves seamless GPU acceleration in part due to Apache Spark’s declarative programming interface. The SQL / Dataframe abstractions are powerful because they separate what a query should produce from how the system should execute it. This enables the cuDF plugin to transparently parallelize row-wise operations using the massive
SIMD
capabilities of GPUs, without any change in user code.
Apache Spark, however, also supports UDFs: custom routines to extend built-in functionality. While useful for implementing bespoke business logic, UDFs break the declarative abstraction—they contain arbitrary user code which the system cannot reason about or parallelize in any general sense. During execution, the GPU accelerator must convert the data from a columnar to row-wise format, and fall back to the CPU to execute the UDF row-by-row:
Figure 1.A CPU UDF forces an otherwise GPU-resident pipeline to convert columnar batches to rows, execute on the CPU, and convert back to columnar format
Thus in an otherwise accelerated query, UDFs have the following drawbacks:
The UDF incurs a round-trip data transfer overhead due to fallback.
The UDF forgoes potential compute speedup, had it been written using GPU-accelerated primitives.
Accelerating UDFs
With a small, targeted code change, many UDFs can be rewritten into a GPU-accelerable form by using the right primitives. Rewriting UDFs eliminates the overhead associated with accelerator fallback, and can yield speedups of
over 20x
.
We outline three approaches to rewrite UDFs:
Approach
Complexity
Best For
SQL
Low, highest level of abstraction
Simple relational logic, e.g. small or inlined functions
cuDF
Medium, more flexibility and control over execution
Most cases, e.g. moderately complex logic like string parsing, nested types
CUDA
High, maximum flexibility and kernel-level control
Most complex or performance critical logic
Table 1. Comparison of SQL, cuDF, and CUDA approaches for rewriting Spark UDFs, organized by complexity and best-fit use case
To make these approaches concrete, consider a simple Scala UDF that converts temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit:
final class ToFahrenheit
extends Function1[java.lang.Double, java.lang.Double]
with Serializable {
override def apply(celsius: java.lang.Double): java.lang.Double = {
if (celsius == null) null
else celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0
}
}
spark.udf.register("to_fahrenheit", new ToFahrenheit)
spark.sql("""
SELECT
*,
to_fahrenheit(celsius) AS fahrenheit
FROM temperatures
""")
Rewriting the UDF with SQL
The most direct solution for simple UDFs is to replace the UDF with an equivalent Spark SQL expression:
spark.sql("""
SELECT
*,
celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0 AS fahrenheit
FROM temperatures
""")
This makes the function visible in Spark’s expression tree. During query planning, the cuDF plugin will replace these expressions with their corresponding GPU implementations, keeping the data and execution fully on the GPU.
Rewriting the UDF with cuDF
When SQL primitives are insufficient or undesirable, the UDF can instead operate directly on GPU columns using the
RapidsUDF
interface, a contract provided by the cuDF plugin. The contract requires a single method,
evaluateColumnar
:
import ai.rapids.cudf.{ColumnVector, Scalar}
import com.nvidia.spark.RapidsUDF
import scala.util.Using
final class ToFahrenheit
extends Function1[java.lang.Double, java.lang.Double]
with Serializable
with RapidsUDF {
override def apply(celsius: java.lang.Double): java.lang.Double = {
if (celsius == null) null
else celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0
}
override def evaluateColumnar(
numRows: Int,
args: ColumnVector*): ColumnVector = {
Using.Manager { use =>
val scale = use(Scalar.fromDouble(9.0 / 5.0))
val offset = use(Scalar.fromDouble(32.0))
val scaled = use(args.head.mul(scale))
scaled.add(offset)
}.get
}
}
The cuDF plugin recognizes instances of the
RapidsUDF
interface and passes a GPU-resident
ColumnVector
to the
evaluateColumnar
function. The function then composes operations from the
Java API for cuDF
operations to process the column in parallel. This approach provides a richer API for more complex processing.
Rewriting the UDF with CUDA
For highly complex logic that cannot be efficiently composed from existing cuDF operations, a
RapidsUDF
can invoke a custom CUDA kernel through the
Java Native Interface (JNI)
. We’ve elided the code for brevity, but examples of CUDA conversions can be found in the
cuDF examples for Spark UDFs
.
Efficient rewrites with AI agents
Despite the performance benefits, UDF rewrites can require significant engineering effort. They demand careful API selection, semantic validation, and performance measurement, while columnar APIs can be unfamiliar to practitioners with less experience in vectorized programming.
Fortunately, much of this work is well suited to coding agents. With proper guardrails, an agent can search unfamiliar APIs, implement candidate rewrites, and iterate quickly while executable tests and performance measurements determine whether each change is acceptable.
Available skills
The cuDF skills for Apache Spark decompose the rewrite into four focused feedback loops. Each skill defines both the work to perform and the evidence required before proceeding to the next stage:
Figure 2. Four skills guide agents through testing, conversion, benchmarking, and optimization, with verification-driven feedback loops at each stage
Scaffolding and design
Reliable agent execution begins with a reliable development environment. The skills provide a complete project template containing the cuDF- and Spark-specific scaffolding required for end-to-end development. This includes test and benchmark harnesses, encoded routines for output verification, and build configuration. By encoding this knowledge into code, the agent can focus on the UDF rather than repeatedly reconstructing specialized infrastructure.
The skills also provide best practices for GPU programming with cuDF, including memory management and configuration. This serves as an advisory tips and tricks reference. To best leverage the power of frontier models, the agent remains free to explore different implementations based on surrounding context and select an approach based on measured correctness and performance.
Performance results
A major consumer technology company used this workflow to convert 30+ UDFs used in production data pipelines into GPU-accelerated implementations. The rewrites preserved the behavior of the original CPU UDFs while removing costly fallbacks from otherwise GPU-accelerated workloads. As an example, the following benchmark shows the resulting before-and-after performance for a UDF in one such workload:
Figure 3. Rewriting a production CPU-based UDF with cuDF reduced operator time from 274.55 to 12.78 hours, a 22x speedup across a 600-billion-row workload
This particular UDF was affecting
more than 3,000+ jobs
, and in this job,
saw a 22x speedup
when implemented as a cuDF-enabled RapidsUDF. With the help of agents, these performance gains are much more attainable, enabling practitioners to iterate on rewrites on the order of hours rather than days or weeks, without compromising correctness.
Get started
Converting UDFs to GPU implementations can unlock major speedups and contribute to overall cost savings in GPU-accelerated pipelines. With agent skills, the rewrite process can be made both
easy and reliable.
To get started, install the
cuDF skills for Apache Spark on GitHub
, either directly or using the
npx
skill installer:
npx skills add NVIDIA/cudf-spark --skill ‘*’
For a deeper walkthrough of the workflow and practical lessons from building it, see the Data + AI Summit session,
Coding with AI Agents to Supercharge Your Spark UDFs with GPU Acceleration
.
To learn more about GPU acceleration for Apache Spark, follow the
cuDF plugin for Apache Spark getting-started guide
to unlock better performance and TCO across your Spark pipelines. Visit our webpage to learn more about
NVIDIA cuDF: GPU-Accelerated Structured Data Processing
, or you can read the docs for more information on
NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark
.

This procedure covers upgrading from Apigee hybrid
version 1.15.x to Apigee hybrid version 1.16.11 and
from previous releases of hybrid 1.16.x to version
1.16.11.
Use the same procedures for minor version upgrades (for example version 1.15
to 1.16) and for patch release upgrades (for example
1.16.0 to 1.16.11).
If you are upgrading from Apigee hybrid version 1.14 or older, you must first upgrade to
hybrid version 1.15 before upgrading to version 1.16.11.
See the instructions for
Upgrading
Apigee hybrid to version 1.15
.
Changes from Apigee hybrid v1.15
Please note the following changes:
Seccomp profiles
:
Starting in
version 1.16
,
Apigee hybrid now offers the capability to apply Seccomp Profiles to your runtime components,
significantly enhancing the security posture of your deployment. This feature allows Apigee
administrators and security teams to restrict the system calls a containerized process can make
to the host's kernel. By limiting a container to only the necessary syscalls, you can:
Enhance Security: Mitigate the risk of container breakouts and privilege escalation.
Enforce Least Privilege: Ensure components only have access to the exact system calls
required for their operation.
Meet Compliance: Provide a critical control for meeting stringent security compliance
requirements.
For more information, see
Configure Seccomp profiles for
pod security
.
UDCA in Apigee hybrid removal
:
In Apigee hybrid
version 1.16
,
the Unified Data Collection Agent (UDCA) component has been removed. The responsibilities of
sending analytics, trace, and deployment status data to the Apigee control plane are now handled
using a
Google Cloud Pub/Sub
based data pipeline. Using the Pub/Sub
based data pipeline has been the default data collection mechanism since Apigee hybrid
version 1.14.0
.
apigee-guardrails
service account
:
In v1.16.0, Apigee Hybrid introduces an
apigee-guardrails
Google IAM service account. This is used by the
apigee-operator
chart during installation to check that all needed APIs are enabled in your project.
See:
Diagnosing issues with guardrails
About service accounts:
apigee-guardrails
create-service-account
Installation Part 2: Step 4: Create service accounts
Installation Part 2: Step 5: Set up service account authentication
Support for cert-manager release 1.18 and 1.19
:
Apigee hybrid v1.16 supports cert-manager
release 1.18
and
release 1.19
. In cert-manager release 1.18, there is a change to the default value of
Certificate.Spec.PrivateKey.rotationPolicy
that can impact traffic. If you are upgrading from a previous version of Apigee hybrid, and you are uprading to cert-manager release 1.18 or above, follow the
Upgrade cert-manager
prodedure in this guide.
Note:
This does not affect fresh installations of Apigee hybrid v1.6.
For additional information about features in Hybrid version 1.16, see the
Apigee hybrid
v1.16.11 release notes
.
Prerequisites
Before upgrading to hybrid version 1.16, make sure your
installation meets the following requirements:
If your hybrid installation is running a version older than v1.15, you
must upgrade to version 1.15 before upgrading to v1.16.
See
Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version 1.15
.
Helm version v3.14.2+.
kubectl
: A supported version of
kubectl
appropriate for your Kubernetes platform version. See
Supported platforms and versions:
kubectl
.
cert-manager: A supported version of cert-manager. See
Supported platforms and versions: cert-manager
. If needed, you will upgrade cert-manager in the
Prepare to upgrade to version 1.16
section below.
Before you upgrade to 1.16.11 - limitations and important notes
Apigee hybrid 1.16.11 introduces a new enhanced per-environment
proxy limit that lets you deploy more proxies and shared flows in a single
environment.  See
Limits: API Proxies
to understand the limits on the number of proxies and shared flows you may deploy per
environment.  This feature is available only on newly created hybrid organizations,
and cannot be applied to upgraded orgs. To use this feature, perform a fresh
installation of hybrid 1.16.11, and create a new organization.
This feature is available exclusively as part of the
2024 subscription plan
,
and is subject to the entitlements granted under that subscription. See
Enhanced per-environment proxy limits
to learn more about this feature.
Upgrading to Apigee hybrid version 1.16 may require
downtime.
When upgrading the Apigee controller to version 1.16.11, all Apigee
deployments undergo a rolling restart. To minimize downtime in production hybrid environments
during a rolling restart, make sure you are running at least two clusters (in the same or
different region/data center). Divert all production traffic to a single cluster and take the
cluster you are about to upgrade offline, and then proceed with the upgrade process. Repeat
the process for each cluster.
Apigee recommends that once you begin the upgrade, you should upgrade all clusters as soon as possible to reduce the chances
of production impact. There is no time limit on when all remaining clusters must be upgraded
after the first one is upgraded. However, until all remaining clusters are upgraded Cassandra
backup and restore cannot work with mixed versions. For example, a backup from Hybrid
1.15 cannot be used to restore a Hybrid 1.16
instance.
Management plane changes do not need to be fully suspended during an upgrade.
Any required temporary suspensions to management plane changes are noted in the upgrade
instructions below.
Upgrading to version 1.16.11 overview
The procedures for upgrading Apigee hybrid are organized in the following sections:
Prepare to upgrade
.
Install hybrid runtime version 1.16.11
.
Prepare to upgrade to version 1.16
Back up your hybrid installation
These instructions use the environment variable
APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME
for the directory
in your file system where you have installed the Helm charts. If needed, change directory
into this directory and define the variable with the following command:
Linux
export APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME=$PWD
echo
$APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME
Mac OS
export APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME=$PWD
echo
$APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME
Windows
set APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME=%CD%
echo %APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME%
Make a backup copy of your version 1.15
$APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME/
directory. You can use any backup process. For example,
you can create a
tar

Conversational analytics, powered by
Gemini for Google Cloud
, lets you investigate your data by asking questions about it in conversational language through an intuitive chat interface. Conversational analytics provides multiple ways to "converse" with your data. When using Conversational Analytics with Explore data, you can ask questions about a single Explore in a conversation or create an Explore data agent to chat with as many as five Explores at once. You can also use Explore data agents that other users have created and shared with you.
Note:
This page refers to Explore data agents — data agents that query Explores. For information about data agents that query user-defined and LookML dashboards, see the
Query a user-defined dashboard with a dashboard agent
and
Create and manage data agents for LookML dashboards
documentation pages, respectively.
This page discusses how to use Conversational Analytics to engage with Explore data. It covers the following topics:
Starting a conversation with a single Explore
Start a conversation with an existing data agent that queries Explores
Asking questions about your data
Managing queries within a conversation
Understanding query results and calculations
Managing conversations
Learn
how and when Gemini
for Google Cloud uses your data
.
As an early-stage technology, Gemini for Google Cloud
products can generate output that seems plausible but is factually incorrect. We recommend that you
validate all output from Gemini for Google Cloud products before you use it.
For more information, see
Gemini for Google Cloud and responsible AI
.
Before you begin
Before you can use Conversational Analytics to engage with your Explore data, make sure that the
setup and requirements for your Looker instance
have been satisfied and that you have been granted the
appropriate permissions
to perform the tasks that are described on this page.
Start a conversation with a single Explore
To start a conversation — a discrete set of questions and answers about your data in regular, natural language in a chat interface — with a single Explore, follow these steps:
Navigate to the Conversational Analytics interface.
From the
main navigation menu
: Select
Conversations
. Select the
Explores
tab and then select the Explore that you want to query.
From the
Create
menu
: Select
Conversation
. Select the
Explores
tab and then select the Explore that you want to query.
From a
Looker Explore
: Select
Start a conversation
. This option isn't available if you're using the
new Explore experience
.
By default the conversation is called "Untitled." After you ask your first question in the conversation, Conversational Analytics automatically generates a conversation title that's based on your question and response. To change the generated name, click the title at the top of the conversation page and enter a new conversation name. To save your changes, click elsewhere on the page, or press return (Mac) or Enter (PC).
Once you have created a conversation, you can
ask questions
about the data in the
send_spark
Ask a question
field within the conversation. You can return to the conversation from the
schedule
Recent Conversations
section.
Start a conversation with an existing data agent that queries Explores
Note:
To create a new data agent to chat with Explore data, see the
Create and manage Explore data agents
documentation page. To query a user-defined or LookML dashboard with a data agent, see the
Query a user-defined dashboard with a dashboard agent
and
Create and manage data agents for LookML dashboards
documentation pages, respectively.
Data agents are customized with context and instructions that are specific to your data. You can start a conversation with an existing
data agent that you created
or that another user has
shared with you
. To start a conversation with an existing data agent that's connected to up to five Looker Explores follow these steps:
Navigate to the Conversational Analytics interface.
From the
main navigation menu
: Select
Conversations
. Select the
Agents
tab and then select the Explore data agent that you want to converse with.
From the
Create
menu
: Select
Conversation
. Select the
Agents
tab and then select the Explore data agent that you want to converse with.
By default the conversation is called "Untitled." After you ask your first question in the conversation, Conversational Analytics automatically generates a conversation title that's based on your question and response. To change the generated name, click the title at the top of the conversation page and enter a new conversation name. To save your changes, click elsewhere on the page, or press return (Mac) or Enter (PC).
Once you have created a conversation, you can
ask questions
about the data in the
send_spark
Ask a question
field within the conversation. You can return to the conversation from the
schedule
Recent Conversations
section.
Ask questions about Looker data
When you're beginning a new conversation, Conversational Analytics suggests some starting questions to ask. The questions don't need to be in a specific format or use a specific syntax. However, they do need to relate to the Explore that you've selected.
Type your question in natural language into the
Ask a question
field. Select a
question mode
and click
send
.
After you submit your query, you can cancel Conversational Analytics's response by clicking
stop
Stop response
. Conversational analytics stops running the query and displays the following message:
The query was cancelled.
For more guidance on the types of questions that you can ask, see
Limitations on questions
.
Select a question mode
When you ask a question, you can select the question mode from a drop-down menu that contains the following options:
Fast
(default): Best for most questions.
Thinking
: Detailed reasoning.
Conversational analytics defaults to
Fast
question mode. Conversational analytics will maintain the same question mode throughout any
multi-turn conversations
, unless you manually change it.
Fast mode
Fast
mode is recommended for most questions and is selected by default. In
Fast
mode, Conversational Analytics maps your natural language query directly to the LookML parameters that are defined in the LookML models that underlie your conversation's Explores. Conversational analytics responds quickly without spending extra tokens on thinking or streaming thoughts summaries in the chat.
Queries in
Fast
mode provide the same level of accuracy as queries in
Thinking
mode. Use
Fast
mode for your questions unless you specifically want to see the agent's reasoning process.
Thinking mode
In
Thinking
mode, the agent spends additional tokens thinking through the request and streams a thoughts summary directly in the chat while processing your query, giving you visibility into the agent's
detailed reasoning
steps.
Although
Thinking
mode does not produce more accurate answers than
Fast
mode, displaying the agent's reasoning lets you observe how Conversational Analytics interprets your query, plans its analytical steps, and references the underlying LookML models.
Select
Thinking
mode if you want to inspect the agent's detailed reasoning steps or test how an agent interacts with your data sources, and you want to spend the additional tokens required for thinking.
How Conversational Analytics processes your questions
Conversational Analytics may rephrase your question after you've submitted a query, and the rephrased question will be displayed in the conversation window following your original question. For example, Conversational Analytics might rephrase the question "What is the mean of user ages?" to "What is the average user age?"
While Conversational Analytics runs your query, you can
observe its reasoning
and thought process. Conversational analytics may ask follow-up questions to clarify any ambiguities in the original query. For example, if there are multiple, similarly named fields, Conversational Analytics may ask you to clarify which field is most appropriate to use in processing your query.
Multi-turn conversations
Conversational Analytics will take previous questions and answers into account as you continue the conversation. You can take previous answers and build on them by further refining results or changing the visualization type.
Important:
You can only reference previous questions in answers from the active conversation. You cannot reference previous questions and answers from other conversations.
For more guidance on creating questions, see
Limitations on questions
.
Clarifying questions
While Conversational Analytics runs your query, you can
observe its reasoning
and thought process. Conversational analytics may ask follow-up questions to clarify any ambiguities in the original query. For example, if there are multiple, similarly named fields, Conversational Analytics may ask you to clarify which field is most appropriate to use in processing your query.
Conversation metadata
When you converse with an Explore or a data agent, the collapsible
storage
Data
panel shows the name of the Looker Explore that's being used by the conversation. The
storage
Data
panel also provides the following options:
open_in_new
View fields
: When chatting with an Explore, you can view the Explore in a new browser window by clicking
open_in_new
View fields
.

items.title: Announcing MCP support in Apigee hybrid: agentic tools that run in your own cluster Apigee hybrid 1.17.0 introduces native Model Context Protocol (MCP) support, enabling the MCP da
items.content:
Announcing MCP support in Apigee hybrid: agentic tools that run in your own cluster
- Google Developers Blog
Announcing MCP support in Apigee hybrid: agentic tools that run in your own cluster
OCT. 14, 2026
Ayo Salawu
Software Engineer
Sundar Ramamoorthy
Software Engineer
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Last December, we
announced preview of MCP support in Apigee
: the ability to turn the APIs you already have, secured, governed and cataloged into tools that AI agents can discover and call, without writing code or standing up MCP servers of your own. The response from customers was immediate and so was the first question back: “
can I have this where my runtime actually lives?”
For many Apigee customers, the runtime does not live on Google-managed infrastructure by accident. It lives in their own data center, in a colocation facility, or in another public cloud because a regulator requires it, because the systems of record are three racks away, or because a multi-cloud estate is simply the reality of the business. Those customers were not asking whether they wanted agentic access to their APIs. They were asking whether they could get it without moving the runtime.
And now they can. With
Apigee hybrid 1.17.0
,
released
on September 14, 2026, Model Context Protocol
support
is available in Apigee hybrid and the MCP data plane runs inside your own Kubernetes cluster.
The same model, in a different place
The conceptual model is the one we shipped on Apigee, unchanged. You describe your API with an OpenAPI 3.0.x specification and create an MCP Discovery Proxy from it. Every operation in that spec becomes an MCP tool. Agents talk to the endpoint over JSON-RPC using
tools/list
to discover what is available and
tools/call
to invoke it and Apigee handles the protocol and the transcoding. You do not write MCP server code and you do not operate an MCP server as a separate piece of software with its own lifecycle.
What changes in hybrid is where the work happens.
In Apigee hybrid, the MCP data plane runs inside your own Kubernetes cluster. The Apigee control plane generates MCP tool configuration from your OpenAPI Specification, your cluster fetches that configuration periodically and MCP request traffic never leaves the cluster.
The diagram below shows where the MCP data plane runs in each deployment model.
Two properties of that architecture are worth stating plainly because they are the ones your security review team will ask about.
MCP request traffic stays inside your cluster.
An agent's
tools/call
request is received, authorized and proxied to your backend entirely within your own infrastructure. No MCP request or response crosses the boundary to Google Cloud at request time.
Configuration is pulled, not pushed.
A sidecar alongside the MCP data plane (from within your cluster) reaches out to fetch the tool configuration derived from your spec. The Apigee control plane (in Google Cloud) never initiates a connection into your cluster, which means MCP requires no inbound path from Google into your network.
What this means for multi-cloud and on-premises
Agentic endpoints run where your APIs already run.
Apigee hybrid already lets you host the runtime on the Kubernetes platform of your choice and MCP inherits that. The MCP sidecar reuses the existing
apigee-watcher
identity. There is no new Google service account to create and no new IAM role to grant. One control-plane grant per organization and the identity you already have does the rest.
Data residency and sovereignty posture carry over.
MCP in Apigee hybrid is available for Subscription and Evaluation organizations, including Data Residency–enabled organizations (configured at organization setup). On hybrid, configuration is fetched from your control plane location and the runtime request path stays in your cluster by construction. For teams whose constraint is "the request may not leave this jurisdiction, this facility, or this VPC," that constraint is supported by the architecture rather than by a setting.
The governance you already wrote applies to agents.
MCP endpoints are Apigee proxies, so they inherit the platform: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, API key verification as well as Apigee's built-in policy library. Tool-level control comes from a concept you already use, the
API product
. You list the specific tool operations a client is entitled to, optionally with a per-tool quota and Apigee enforces it. It also filters discovery automatically. When a client calls
tools/list
, the response contains only the tools in that client's API product. An agent cannot call
delete_account
if it was never allowed to see it.
Your agentic traffic shows up where your API traffic does.
Deployed MCP Discovery Proxies are automatically ingested into Apigee API hub, assigned the
MCP
API style and their operations mapped to individual tools a searchable catalog that developers can query in natural language rather than a spreadsheet of endpoints. In API insights, two filters,
API style
and
MCP tool name
let you isolate agentic traffic from ordinary REST traffic and look at a single tool across the API performance, error analysis, latency and target performance dashboards. You can see the ratio of discovery to execution and you can tell proxy overhead apart from backend time.
Turning it on
MCP is an optional feature in Apigee hybrid and is not enabled by default. Enabling it is a Helm operation on a cluster already running Apigee hybrid 1.17.0 or later. Steps to do this are as follows.
Set the top-level enableMcpServer: true key in your overrides.yaml, then upgrade the apigee-operator chart first and the apigee-org chart second. The order matters. The operator chart owns the schema for the new MCP resources and upgrading in the wrong order produces a successful upgrade with no MCP pods. There is also a one-time, per-organization grant that adds the apigee-watcher identity to your organization's control plane access, so the sidecar can retrieve configuration. Defaults are sensible out of the box. Two MCP replicas, autoscaling to ten. Rolling back is the same field set to false and a single chart upgrade.
A few things to plan for before you schedule the change. Enabling or disabling MCP triggers a staged canary release of runtime pods, so run it in an approved maintenance window. The public documentation
here
describes how to enable MCP in an existing Apigee hybrid cluster.
Observing MCP Traffic within Apigee
Your MCP proxy is exposed as a single endpoint. Every agent request, whatever tool it invokes, arrives at the same /mcp path. Apigee tags each of those requests with the name of the tool that was called, so API insights can break that one endpoint out by tool and show which tools your agents actually used, how often and over what period. The screenshot below shows API insights, including requests to the MCP proxy (mcp) and also see individual tools (as API proxies mcp-healthcare, mcp-petstore, mcp-statuscode) response time and tps. See public documentation on monitoring and analyzing mcp traffic with Apigee API insights
here
and
here
on how to use the API insights dashboard.
We also have a view of tools being called in the tool performance tab within API insights below.
What's next: tracing an agent's call end to end
An MCP tool call crosses an AI client, Apigee and your backend. Today each of those is its own island of logs, so the question platform teams actually ask “where did the time go?” has no single answer.
The snippet below is an example mcp tools call request from an AI client. The curl request below allows for end to end tracking of the request, when distributed trace is enabled in Apigee with OTEL.
curl -X POST "https://xxx.xxx.xxx.net/mcp" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-H "MCP-Protocol-Version: 2025-11-25" \
-d '{
"jsonrpc": "2.0",
"id": 321,
"method": "tools/call",
"params": {
"name": "createReward",
"arguments": {
"reward": "123"
},
"_meta": {
"traceparent": "00-3ad8012d970b3971cb16cda653a1a370-df3047d1d0830dc0-01"
}
}
}'
Shell
Copied
The same call as orchestrated by distributed trace in Google CloudTrace shows the calls in its entirety in one global view. (Assumption is all services (Apigee/Non-Apigee) in the chain report to the same Google CloudTrace)
MCP clients carry W3C trace context inside the JSON-RPC _meta field, which a conventional REST backend has no idea how to read. Apigee extracts it and forwards it as ordinary traceparent and tracestate headers, so instrumented services downstream join the trace without code changes. Three things follow: a single trace ID spanning the AI client, the Apigee proxies and backend execution; backends that participate without recoding and less noise, because the gateway can forward context in passthrough mode rather than emitting infrastructure spans of its own which also trims trace ingestion cost.
The ecosystem is converging on the same idea.
SEP-2028
, an open proposal in the MCP community, aims to standardize _meta-to-header forwarding of W3C trace context standard behavior for MCP servers.
The OpenTelemetry path that carries W3C trace context is available in Apigee today.
Next steps
MCP support is available now in Apigee hybrid 1.17.0. Start with the
MCP in Apigee overview
for the architecture,
Enable MCP in Apigee hybrid
for the Helm procedure and the
MCP quickstart
to get a first tool answering an agent.

items.title: Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics Gemini 4 Argon is a general-purpose physical reasoning model designed to enhance workflows across the robotics stack with advanced capabilities in physi
items.content:
Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics
- Google Developers Blog
Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics
OCT. 13, 2026
Kanishka Rao
Principal Software Engineer
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Gemini 4 Argon marks a step change in physical understanding, code generation, and visual-semantic reasoning—unlocking new workflows across the robotics stack and accelerating progress toward physical AGI.
You can see this leap in capability on the
Embodied Reasoning (ERQA) benchmark
, which tests a model's ability to understand and solve physical, spatial problems in 3D environments. Using pure reasoning, Argon scores 87%, outperforming every other frontier model.
As a general-purpose physical reasoning model, Argon can be applied across the entire robotics lifecycle. In this post, we share representative prompts for Argon across four key areas:
Robot control →
Mobile manipulation with
MuJoCo
practice, zero-shot robot control, and closed-loop steering of video world models.
Real2Sim →
Reconstructing physically calibrated simulation twins from robot camera feeds, egocentric human video, or hand-drawn paper sketches.
Physical understanding →
Agentic multimodal hindsight labeling including detailed understanding of dexterity, dense value functions and progress estimation.
Research and self-improvement →
Action improvement via simulation and iterative self-improvement on hardware.
Unlocking robot control with Argon
1. Spot mobile manipulation: Putting in the trash bin with MuJoCo practice
Argon controls a Boston Dynamics Spot® quadruped (12-DoF legs + 6-DoF arm) to learn a new skill: stepping on a foot-pedal trash bin to throw away soda cans. Argon creates an articulated MuJoCo digital twin of a foot-pedal trash bin to practice its moves before stepping on the physical pedal and dropping soda cans into the open bin.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Spot Mobile Manipulation — Real-to-Sim-to-Real foot-pedal trash bin disposal: Spot picking up the soda can, checking its wrist camera, practicing 3-leg tripod balance in MuJoCo, stepping on the foot pedal, verifying hand centering in the open bin, and dropping the can inside.
Prompt:
There's a Diet Coke can behind you and another on the black table on your left.
Use the spot-mobile-manipulation skill to pick them up and trash them in the black foot-pedal bin.
Before stepping down on the pedal, verify in the front cameras that your front-right foot target is centered on the pedal, and use a 2-agent verification swarm (foot-verifier and hand-verifier) to verify both the foot-pedal step and the 3D hand-in-bin alignment before releasing.
Plain text
Copied
2. Zero-shot control
Argon controls a simple robotic arm to place a fallen mug upright and put the crumpled napkin inside. Argon reasons with a visual coordinate harness and action primitives to perform this task over several turns.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Left: 3rd-person real robot view; Right: calibrated wrist camera with projected 2 cm world coordinates and jaw-closing reticle.
Prompt:
[Attached: wrist_cam.png, obs.json]
Task: Get the robot arm to reorient the mug upright and put the napkin inside the mug.
## Execution Discipline
- Simply output 1 sentence observation followed immediately by your `curl` command (with `# Plan:` on Turn 1 and `# Thought:` on every turn). Everything needed is in `obs.json` and the calibrated reticle/grid drawn on `wrist_cam.png`.
## Visual Coordinate Reference (Annotated on wrist_cam.png)
- `+X` (UP in image): Away from robot base | `-X` (DOWN): Towards robot base
- `+Y` (LEFT in image): World left         | `-Y` (RIGHT): World right
- `+Z`: Height above table                | `Yellow numbers`: World (X, Y) in centimetres (2 cm grid at `grid_z`)
- `Cyan + crosshair`: Current 3D pinch center
- `Cyan [ + ] brackets`: Current jaw opening and closing line
- `Green line`: Current object long-axis orientation (`yaw_deg`: 0° = vertical along +X, 90° = horizontal along +Y)
- `pitch_deg = 90°`: Straight down (-Z) top-down grasp/place; `pitch_deg < 60°`: Tilted coaxial approach along finger axis
## Closed-Loop Turn Workflow
1. Inspect current state & view `wrist_cam.png`:
`curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8081/obs` (returns `ee_pos`, `holding`, `status`, `workspace`, `wrist_cam_path`).
2. Select VLM call granularity upfront on Turn 1:
- Coarse (2–4 calls): `look_at` -> `grasp` -> `place` -> `done`
- Pre-Grasp Hover Verify (4–7 calls): `look_at` -> `goto(z=0.04)` (verify cyan `[ + ]` brackets straddle target) -> `grasp` -> `place_until_contact` -> `done`
- Fine Visual Servoing (8–20 calls): `look_at` -> `grasp` -> pre-pose `goto` -> closed-loop `move_by` / `move_until_contact` -> `done`
3. Send motion primitives (`POST /plan`) and verify visually after every turn in the updated `wrist_cam.png`. If `status == "grasp_failed"`, call `robot.look_at(...)` to re-observe and recover closed-loop.
## Code-as-Policies Primitives (`POST http://127.0.0.1:8081/plan`)
robot.look_at(x=0.35, y=0.13, z=0.14, grid_z=0.015)
x, y = robot.deproject(u=0.52, v=0.48, z_plane=0.015)
robot.grasp(x=x, y=y, z=0.015, yaw_deg=-35, pitch_deg=90)
robot.place(x=0.24, y=0.06, z=0.075)
robot.place_until_contact(x=0.24, y=0.06, z=0.015, max_lag=0.012, relief=0.002)
robot.goto(x=0.28, y=0.05, z=0.04, arc_z=0.14, pitch_deg=25, azimuth_deg=90, roll_deg=0, speed=0.10)
robot.move_by(forward=0.025, dz=-0.002, dpitch_deg=-3, droll_deg=5, speed=0.04)
robot.move_until_contact(dz=-0.06, speed=0.03, max_lag=0.012, relief=0.002)
robot.open_gripper() / robot.close_gripper() / robot.home() / robot.done()
Plain text
Copied
3. Omni control
Argon steers robots in the Gemini Omni World Model to rearrange five scattered Scrabble tiles (
G, R, A, N, O
) into a clean row spelling
A - R - G - O - N
. Instead of specifying one static prompt, Argon steers in a closed visual loop. It writes timestamped action prompts, inspecting intermediate rollout keyframes, and refining its prompts.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Iterative Video World Model Steering Dexterous Hands: 33-Step Steered Video Rollout Spelling A-R-G-O-N.
Prompt:
Goal: {task_goal}
You are steering a video world model (Gemini Omni) in an iterative visual feedback loop. Inspect the attached frames from the latest rollout and write the next timestamped action prompt for the video world model:
- Break complex motions into one simple, single-direction action at a time.
- Keep inactive hands retracted and avoid blocking the camera's view of objects in the workspace.
- Explicitly state which areas of the workspace become empty after an object moves.
- Use [MM:SS.mmm] timestamps for each action beat and wrap your output in <omni_prompt> tags.
Example format (sample timestamps only, not the full prompt):
<omni_prompt>
[00:00.000] Character A's left hand rests at the side while the right hand reaches toward the target object.
[00:02.500] Character A's right fingertips push the object smoothly into the center of the table, leaving its starting area empty.
[00:05.000] Character A's right hand opens and retracts to the side so all placed objects remain in clear view of the camera.
</omni_prompt>
Plain text
Copied
Unlocking Real2Sim with Argon
1. Robot view to simulation
Argon views a real robot teleoperation episode and develops a digital twin; it obtains or creates simulation assets that look and behave like the real objects upon contact with the dexterous hands.
